findings.statement: CXCR2 tops the convergence ranking, yet the verbatim-checked relation layer holds no relation for it. The corpus has only title and abstract sentences: one titled 'CXCR1 and CXCR2 are potential neutrophil extracellular trap-related treatment targets in ulcerative colitis: insights from Mendelian randomization, colocalization and transcriptomic analysis', and one reporting that the CXCL5/CXCR2 axis was involved in neutrophil chemotaxis and immune activation in UC. Open Targets lists clinical-stage CXCR2 antagonists, but no UC trial appears in these records. In the eight-cohort meta-analysis CXCR2 ranks [gene=CXCR2; type=rank_context; source=ANALYSIS:rank_context; rank=68] of the increased genes, and its Open Targets association rank is [gene=CXCR2; type=rank_context; source=ANALYSIS:rank_context; rank=25] among genes in the graph.

One paper states that the CXCL8 axis acting through CXCR1 and CXCR2 participates in the pathogenesis of UC through multiple signaling pathways, including MAPKs and NF-kappaB. A blood RNA-seq validation cohort reported CXCL8 among the genes with the highest diagnostic performance for IBD. Evidence is bioinformatic and review-level.

A single study reports IDO1 expression elevated in UC patients and correlated with classically activated macrophage polarization. It also reports that IDO1 induced this polarization via the ER stress-associated GRP78-XBP pathway to promote UC progression, and that a tryptophan-analogue IDO1 inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis in mice. This is preclinical, single-study evidence.

MMP1 transcripts are modified by mirikizumab and correlate with UC disease activity indices (modified Mayo, Geboes, Robarts Histopathology Index), alongside MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B. Another study calls MMP1 a hub gene associated with macrophage infiltration, and a third reports strong diagnostic potential for UC-associated CRC. This suggests a treatment-response and activity marker that is mostly expression-based.

CHI3L1 was significantly upregulated in UC patients and strongly correlated with NLRP3 inflammasome expression. One study reports that CHI3L1 promotes macrophage pyroptosis via the BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis. Velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 was confirmed in vitro by microscale thermophoresis. This is early preclinical work.

DUOX2 protein was among the most elevated in inflamed UC biopsies relative to healthy controls (with HLA-DRA, CD74 and lipocalin-2). DUOX2 is also listed among credible potential diagnostic biomarkers for UC, and IBD and CRC share increased DUOX2 expression. One herbal formula study states that DUOX2 may serve as a key therapeutic target. Evidence is mostly bioinformatic and observational.

One study reports that the receiver operating characteristic curve demonstrates excellent performance of S100A9 expression in diagnosing active UC. ONT-RNA-seq also found S100A9 significantly higher in UC. In a single-cell treatment-response study, S100A9 was down-regulated in resident macrophages in responders.

IL1B is listed among credible diagnostic biomarkers for UC. In a tofacitinib study, non-responders showed expansion and activation of macrophages and fibroblasts after treatment, with upregulation of MMP9, IL1B, IL6, CXCL1, CXCL8 and S100A9 versus baseline. This suggests a macrophage-derived non-response signature, which comes from infiltrating immune cells rather than epithelial change.

CXCL1 appears as a biomarker candidate in several machine-learning and bioinformatic studies. It is one of five pivotal genes whose combined diagnostic model reached a much higher AUC than the individual genes, which each exceeded only a modest threshold. In another study CXCL1 was a weaker activity marker than CYP2R1, LPCAT1 and NEU4.
HMGCS2 expression decreased in UC (with AQP8) in two separate studies, and one states these genes have high diagnostic value for UC. This supports an epithelial metabolic loss signature.
ONT-RNA-seq found SLC26A3 significantly lower in UC patients compared to the normal control group, consistent with an epithelial transport loss signature.

LCN2 expression was higher in UC than normal, and higher in short-duration than long-duration UC, than UC-associated cancer. One study proposes it as a diagnostic biomarker for UC-associated carcinogenesis related to disease duration. LCN2 is also reported among genes shared as increased by IBD and CRC.

caveats: CXCR1, CXCR2, CD274, JAK2, FCGR2A and INHBA have strong expression or genetic support in the ranking but no verbatim-checked literature relation in this corpus, so literature support is silent or indirect for them. CD274 finding was removed for that reason.
Most biomarker claims come from bioinformatic hub-gene or machine-learning studies of public datasets, often with limited independent validation.
Drug stages from Open Targets are not UC-specific; drug names without a peer-reviewed paper record were left out.
Tofacitinib non-response signature (macrophage/fibroblast) comes from one single-cell study.
No claim is made about whether HMGCS2 or CHI3L1 have approved drugs; the records do not state it.
